todays_goal: Begin Week 2 with precise vocabulary, self-contained questions, and forward progress where Friday showed readiness.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.previous_learning: Friday showed strong light-path reasoning but inconsistent material classification. Wax paper transmitted light without a clear image, yet was labeled transparent.
lessons.course_context: Repair the classification vocabulary needed for the Light and Matter unit.
learning_objectives: Classify materials using transmission and image clarity.
lessons.why_it_matters: Precise classification is necessary for explaining how light interacts with matter.

vocabulary.definition: let light pass through
redirect light in many directions
transmits most visible light with little scattering, so a clear image forms
transmits some visible light but scatters it, so images are blurry
does not transmit visible light
an observation used to support an explanation

lessons.written_instruction: Use two tests: does visible light pass through, and if so does a clear image form? Transparent preserves detail, translucent transmits but scatters, and opaque blocks visible light.

worked_examples.title: Transparent
worked_examples.explanation: Light passes and a sharp image remains.

worked_examples.title: Translucent
worked_examples.explanation: Light passes but scattering blurs details.

guided_practice.prompt: Frosted glass lets light through but you cannot see a sharp image. Classify it and explain using transmission and image clarity.
guided_practice.hint: Light passes, but details are blurred.

guided_practice.prompt: A black poster board blocks a flashlight beam. Classify it and state the observation that supports your answer.
A clear plastic ruler lets you read print sharply through it. Classify it and explain.

independent_practice.prompt: A lampshade glows when the lamp is on, but the bulb is not seen sharply through the shade. Classify the material and explain.
Explain the difference between transmitting light and forming a clear image.
Why can a translucent material make a room brighter even when you cannot see a clear object through it?

exit_ticket.prompt: Wax paper lets visible light through but makes printed letters blurry. Name the material class and explain why.
exit_ticket.answer: Translucent; it transmits light but scatters it so the image is unclear.

exit_ticket.prompt: In one sentence, explain what scattering does to light.
exit_ticket.answer: Scattering redirects light in many directions.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach with the two-test rule. Connect to Friday's wax-paper observation. Ask self-contained questions naming the material; never use vague referents such as 'the second one.'
lessons.teacher_notes: Friday evidence: light path strong; classification/scattering needs repair.

lessons.subject: french
lessons.lesson_title: Etre and avoir with negation review
lessons.previous_learning: Friday showed generally accurate regular -ER conjugation and improving ne...pas/elision.
lessons.course_context: Move from regular -ER verbs into high-frequency irregular verbs.
learning_objectives: Apply elision in n'ai and n'est.
lessons.why_it_matters: These verbs appear constantly in French.

vocabulary.definition: to be
to have
a verb that does not follow the regular -ER pattern
change a verb to match the subject
a form such as ne...pas
dropping a vowel before another vowel sound

lessons.written_instruction: Teach etre: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous etes, ils/elles sont; avoir: j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont. Review ne...pas and elision.

guided_practice.prompt: Complete with etre: Nous ___ prets.
Complete with avoir: Ils ___ deux livres.
Make negative: J'ai un crayon.
Make negative: Elle est contente.

independent_practice.prompt: Answer in a complete French sentence: Est-ce que tu as un livre aujourd'hui?
Answer in a complete French sentence: Est-ce que tu es fatigue ce matin?
Write one true sentence with nous sommes.

lessons.voice_prompt: Use natural pronunciation, short exchanges, and explicit sentence references. Correct one or two high-value errors at a time.

lessons.subject: mathematics
lessons.previous_learning: Friday decimal division was accurate across guided, independent, application, and exit-ticket work.
lessons.course_context: Begin the Grade 6 ratios unit while retaining short decimal-fluency review.
lessons.why_it_matters: Ratios are the foundation for unit rates, proportional reasoning, percent, and scale.

vocabulary.definition: a comparison of two quantities by division
ratios that describe the same comparison
one part compared with another
one part compared with the entire group
the number used to multiply or divide both quantities
a table of equivalent ratio pairs

lessons.written_instruction: Order matters. Ratios can be written 3 to 5, 3:5, or 3/5. Equivalent ratios multiply or divide both quantities by the same nonzero factor.

guided_practice.prompt: A tray has 4 red tiles and 7 white tiles. Write red to white in three forms.
The same tray has 11 tiles total. Write red to all tiles.
Complete 3:8 = 6:__. State the scale factor.
For 2 notebooks per 5 pencils, complete (2,5), (4,__),(6,__),(8,__).

independent_practice.prompt: A model kit has 6 metal pieces and 9 plastic pieces. Write metal to plastic in simplest form.
The same kit has 15 pieces total. Write plastic to all pieces in simplest form.
A paint mixture uses 3 parts blue for every 4 parts white. If 12 parts white are used, how many blue? Show an equivalent-ratio method.
A snack mix uses 5 cups cereal for every 2 cups nuts. Find nuts for 10 cups cereal and 15 cups cereal.
Are 4:6 and 10:15 equivalent? Show how you know.

exit_ticket.prompt: A shelf has 8 fiction books and 12 nonfiction books. What is fiction to nonfiction in simplest form?
Write one ratio equivalent to 5:7 and state the scale factor.
Explain why 2:3 and 4:5 are not equivalent.
exit_ticket.answer: No single scale factor changes both quantities; the ratios have different values.

lessons.voice_prompt: Begin with 6.3 divided by 0.9 and 4.8 divided by 0.6 as a five-minute check, then teach ratios. Always name both quantities in ratio questions.
lessons.teacher_notes: Friday supports moving forward to ratios.

lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.previous_learning: Friday showed a strong geography-to-polis chain, with a few incomplete details.
lessons.course_context: Move from why poleis formed to how different poleis developed distinct systems.
learning_objectives: Explain shared culture without one government.
Describe limits of Athenian political participation.
lessons.why_it_matters: Comparing poleis shows cultural connection alongside political difference.

vocabulary.definition: a Greek polis known for trade, civic debate, arts, and early democracy for male citizens
a Greek polis known for military organization and strict social discipline
a recognized member of a political community
government in which citizens participate in political decisions
government controlled by a small group

lessons.written_instruction: Use the assigned source. Clarify that ancient Athenian democracy excluded women, enslaved people, and many residents. Compare specific institutions and priorities.

worked_examples.title: Similarity
worked_examples.problem: What did Athens and Sparta share?
worked_examples.solution: Greek language, religion, festivals, and wider culture.
worked_examples.explanation: Shared culture did not require one government.

worked_examples.title: Difference
worked_examples.solution: Athens involved male citizens more directly; Sparta concentrated authority more narrowly.

guided_practice.prompt: Name two cultural features Athens and Sparta shared.
How did government participation in Athens differ from political power in Sparta?

independent_practice.prompt: Why is it inaccurate to say ancient Athenian democracy gave equal political rights to everyone living in Athens?
What larger idea about the Greek world is shown by the differences between Athens and Sparta?

exit_ticket.prompt: In 3-4 sentences, compare Athens and Sparta. Include one similarity, one difference, and explain how this supports the idea that Greek poleis were culturally connected but politically independent.
exit_ticket.answer: Answers vary; must include all three parts.

lessons.voice_prompt: Give map and chronology context first. Use explicit subjects in every question; avoid vague referents.

lessons.subject: literature
lessons.previous_learning: Friday informational reading showed improved topic, central idea, and objective summary precision.
lessons.course_context: Begin fiction-focused work on inference, conflict, character, and universal theme.
lessons.why_it_matters: These skills support novel study and literary analysis.

vocabulary.definition: the reason a character chooses to act
a conclusion based on evidence plus reasoning
a struggle or problem driving a story
a complete message about life, people, or choices
a specific detail supporting an interpretation

lessons.written_instruction: Read 'The Spare Key.' Require a specific action or line for inference. Theme must be transferable and should not use a character name.

worked_examples.title: Inference
worked_examples.problem: A character hides a broken tool, later admits it, and helps repair it.
worked_examples.solution: The character may value honesty more after seeing consequences.
worked_examples.explanation: The inference connects actions to motivation.

worked_examples.title: Theme
worked_examples.solution: Taking responsibility for mistakes can help people improve systems and rebuild trust.
worked_examples.explanation: The message applies beyond one character.

guided_practice.prompt: What is Malik's main problem at the beginning of 'The Spare Key'?
What does Malik consider doing instead of admitting he lost the key, and what does that reveal about his immediate motivation?

independent_practice.prompt: Why is Malik's decision to tell the truth important to the plot? Use one event that happens afterward.
What can you infer about Priya from her response after Malik admits the problem? Use one detail.
What larger lesson has Malik drawn from the mistake?
Write a universal theme statement without using a character's name.
Give two pieces of evidence supporting your theme.
Write a 3-sentence objective summary.

exit_ticket.prompt: What is the difference between a topic such as mistakes and a theme about mistakes?
exit_ticket.answer: A topic names the subject; a theme states a complete, transferable message about it.

lessons.voice_prompt: Do not reveal the theme. Ask which exact action or line supports each inference. Keep questions self-contained.

lessons.subject: writing
lessons.previous_learning: Friday's bridge paragraph showed strong content, evidence, and reasoning; punctuation and sentence boundaries were the main weakness.
lessons.course_context: Keep the strong reasoning while making sentence structure clearer.
learning_objectives: Write a short explanation with clear cause/effect.
lessons.why_it_matters: Clear sentence boundaries make strong ideas easy to understand.

vocabulary.definition: a group of words expressing a complete thought
two or more complete thoughts joined without correct punctuation
two complete sentences joined only with a comma
a connecting word such as and, but, so, or because

lessons.written_instruction: Teach period and conjunction repairs. Do not rewrite Atticus's paragraph for him.

worked_examples.title: Run-on
worked_examples.problem: The metal warms it expands the joint gives it room to move.
worked_examples.solution: The metal warms and expands. The joint gives it room to move.

worked_examples.title: Comma splice
worked_examples.problem: The model was confident, it was still wrong.
worked_examples.solution: The model was confident, but it was still wrong.
worked_examples.explanation: A conjunction correctly joins the ideas.

guided_practice.prompt: Repair: The bridge gets warmer the metal expands the sections need room to move.
Repair: The classifier showed 99% confidence, the prediction was incorrect.
Combine with because: Wax paper is translucent. It transmits light but scatters it.

independent_practice.prompt: Write one sentence explaining why punctuation can change how easily a reader understands an idea.

Write 6-8 sentences explaining why a good system is designed so one person's mistake does not automatically cause the whole process to fail. Use 'The Spare Key' as one example and include cause/effect.

exit_ticket.prompt: What is one way to fix a run-on sentence?
exit_ticket.answer: Separate complete thoughts with correct punctuation or join them with an appropriate conjunction.

lessons.voice_prompt: Acknowledge Friday's strong ideas/evidence, then focus narrowly on sentence boundaries. Name the exact sentence being revised.

lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.previous_learning: Friday showed good generalization understanding, but confidence-versus-correctness explanations remained vague.
lessons.course_context: Continue AI literacy by evaluating model outputs and training-data variety.
learning_objectives: Describe how narrow training data weakens generalization.
Use before/after evidence from a classifier test.
lessons.why_it_matters: AI systems can be confident and wrong; evaluation matters.

vocabulary.definition: the class or output a model chooses
how strongly the model matches an input to one of its learned classes
whether the prediction is actually right
working well on new examples not seen exactly during training
examples used to teach a model

lessons.written_instruction: Use the concrete example: actual object BOOK; model predicts CUP at 99%. That prediction is wrong. The confidence score describes model preference among known classes, not truth.

worked_examples.title: Varied training
worked_examples.problem: 30 identical cup photos vs varied angles/backgrounds
worked_examples.explanation: The model sees more possible appearances.

guided_practice.prompt: A classifier sees a book but predicts CUP with 99% confidence. Is the prediction correct, and what does the 99% mean?
Why might a classifier trained only on cups photographed on a white table perform worse outdoors?

independent_practice.prompt: Which training set is more likely to generalize: 30 nearly identical cup photos, or 30 varied cup photos? Explain.
If you run a Teachable Machine test, name the single condition changed and record prediction/confidence before and after.
Use the evidence to decide whether generalization was strong or weak.

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain why high model confidence does not guarantee a correct prediction.
exit_ticket.answer: Confidence shows model preference among learned classes; the chosen class can still be wrong.

exit_ticket.prompt: Name one training-data change that could improve generalization.
exit_ticket.answer: Add more varied and representative examples.

lessons.voice_prompt: Use concrete named objects, classes, and confidence values. Avoid vague references such as 'the second condition.'

lessons.subject: art_design
lessons.previous_learning: Friday's Art/Design block was not attempted because the day was shortened for a doctor appointment. It is carryover, not remediation.
lessons.course_context: Begin the Art/Design portfolio with a visual explainer.
learning_objectives: Create a central diagram with annotations.
lessons.why_it_matters: Visual communication transfers to science, design, and presentations.

vocabulary.definition: the order in which a viewer notices information
a short label explaining part of a visual
a difference that helps important elements stand out
the arrangement of elements
brief text explaining a visual

lessons.written_instruction: Choose one learned concept. Plan what the viewer should notice first, one main visual, three annotations, and a 2-3 sentence caption.

guided_practice.prompt: Choose one concept you want to teach visually and name the intended viewer.
What should the viewer notice first?

independent_practice.prompt: Create a one-page visual explainer with a clear title, one main visual, at least three annotations, deliberate hierarchy, and a 2-3 sentence caption.

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain how your use of size or contrast created visual hierarchy.
exit_ticket.answer: Answers vary; explain what is emphasized first and how.

lessons.voice_prompt: This is carryover from Friday's shortened day and carries no penalty. Do not design it for him.
